title: Short Stuff: BM Radio
summary: Short Stuff episode on "beautiful music" (BM radio), a soft, orchestral easy-listening radio format. The hosts explain that FM radio was initially considered square and AM was the popular band, and that FM's early programming gave rise to easy listening. They cover a 1965 FCC ruling requiring AM and FM stations in common ownership to play different programming, which pushed companies toward BM. They describe the format's targeting of housewives, its limits on ads (about six minutes per hour, quieter than the music), and syndicator Shulkey Radio Productions (SRP), which supplied prerecorded tapes and technical standards. They also cover Bonneville's automated random tape-selection system, the format's spread and decline as rock grew, and comparisons to Atlanta's 99X and WKRP in Cincinnati.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts open the short episode and introduce the topic of radio, contrasting AM and FM reputations.

segments.title: AM vs FM and what beautiful music is
segments.summary: The hosts explain that FM started out square and AM was the popular band, and that FM gave rise to easy listening. They describe beautiful music: pop and standards rearranged for orchestra with vocals mostly removed, and occasionally covers sung by groups like the Ray Conniff Singers.

segments.title: Does everyone like beautiful music?
segments.summary: Hosts discuss whether the genre appeals broadly, noting that some well-done covers, such as a version of 'What's New Pussycat', are good even if the format itself is not universally loved.

segments.title: 1965 FCC ruling and the housewife audience
segments.summary: A 1965 FCC ruling required stations with separate AM and FM programming to play different content, which pushed companies toward beautiful music as a cheap way to differentiate. The format targeted housewives, who made household purchasing decisions.

segments.title: Format's ad limits and Shulkey Radio Productions
segments.summary: Beautiful music kept ads limited and quiet. Shulkey Radio Productions (SRP) became the biggest syndicator, supplying prerecorded tapes with requirements for equipment, engineers, ad limits of about six minutes per hour at lower volume, and restrictions on attention-grabbing ads. Hosts note the science behind the programming was questionable.

segments.title: Playlist looping and Bonneville's random tape player
segments.summary: Shulkey's playlists looped, so Bonneville offered prerecorded tapes plus an automatic random tape player that varied the sequence of songs, avoiding identical repeats.

segments.title: Format's spread and decline
segments.summary: Beautiful music was the cradle of radio standardization and automation and spread to most cities. As rock grew and younger listeners became the main audience, stations switched formats. Hosts compare this to 99X in Atlanta's switch to alternative music.

segments.title: Atlanta left-of-dial stations
segments.summary: Hosts reminisce about Atlanta's Album 88 and other left-of-the-dial stations, comparing them to WFMU in New Jersey, and mention Adam Bomb's Soul Kitchen show.

segments.title: WKRP in Cincinnati reference
segments.summary: Beautiful music stations dropping by 1990 is dramatized in WKRP in Cincinnati, where a station converts from beautiful music to rock.

segments.title: WKRP wrap-up
segments.summary: Hosts recall WKRP characters reacting to the rock format change.

segments.summary: Hosts thank their sources and sign off.
